claims.text: Conventional arc-melting produces the titanium- and nickel-containing HEA as a single-phase solid solution with typical oxygen and nitrogen pickup.
Replacing conventional arc-melting with ultra-high-vacuum melting will minimize oxygen and nitrogen contamination during synthesis.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen can promote phase segregation during elevated-temperature aging.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will prevent impurity-induced nanoscale phase segregation.
Reducing interstitial impurities will prevent precipitate-depleted zones near grain boundaries.
Impurity-assisted phase segregation depletes strengthening solutes from the metal matrix.
Depletion of interstitial strengthening solutes during aging causes progressive mechanical softening.
Lower impurity levels will maintain a more chemically uniform microstructure at elevated temperatures.
A more chemically uniform microstructure will preserve the alloy's inherent high-temperature strength.
The UHV-processed titanium- and nickel-containing HEA will retain a more homogeneous single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures than the arc-melted counterpart.
The UHV-processed alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the conventionally processed alloy.
The UHV-processed alloy will show better overall mechanical performance under extreme-environment testing.
The conventionally processed baseline undergoes impurity-related microstructural softening at high temperature.
The comparison should keep alloy composition, phase state, fabrication conditions other than melting atmosphere, and mechanical-test regime constant.
The hypothesis is restricted to a titanium- and nickel-containing HEA in a single-phase solid-solution state under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing.
Prior evidence qualitatively supports controlling interstitial impurities to limit high-temperature softening.
The magnitude of any strength enhancement is uncertain without quantitative impurity measurements and mechanical testing.
